articles.title: Microbes at the end of the Earth: Antarctica's hidden biodiversity
articles.dek: When we think about Antarctica, many people imagine penguins, seals and whales. However, the majority of Antarctica's scientific wonders cannot be seen without a microscope.
paragraphs: When we think about Antarctica, many people imagine penguins, seals and whales. However, the majority of Antarctica's scientific wonders cannot be seen without a microscope. These microbial communities form the foundation of Antarctic ecosystems yet remain largely invisible to most visitors.

Recent research published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showed that some microbes living in Antarctic soils appear to exist nowhere else on Earth. This challenges scientists' long-held belief that microbes are easily dispersed and therefore found everywhere.

Antarctica is one of the Earth's most isolated and harsh environments. Its organisms have to deal with extreme cold, dryness, intense UV radiation and limited nutrients, creating selective pressures unique to the continent. Soil temperatures can range from around 8°C (46 degrees Fahrenheit) during the summer to below -25°C (-13 degrees Fahrenheit) in winter while air temperatures can fall below -40°C (-40 degrees Fahrenheit). Rapid temperature fluctuations are common, which creates particularly challenging conditions for life.

While extreme cold also occurs in the Arctic, it is the historical geographical isolation that characterizes evolution to the cold in the Antarctic. Antarctic species have been effectively isolated in the cold from the rest of the planet by the circumpolar current for 10–15 million years, whereas the Arctic is still highly connected to other continents and has been cold for only around 1. 5 million years .

The researchers studied strains of the bacterium Arthrobacter from Antarctica and compared them with samples from other cold and dry environments, such as the Atacama Desert, Svalbard and the Tibetan Plateau. They found distinct Antarctic strains that seem to have evolved in isolation on the continent, suggesting Antarctica's conditions have allowed unique microbial communities to develop over long periods.

The fact that Antarctica may be home to organisms found nowhere else raises important questions about evolution, conservation and biotechnology—and particularly how we can preserve such cold-adapted biodiversity in a warming world.
These microbes are not simply biological curiosities. They play a fundamental role in nutrient cycling and form the base of Antarctic food webs.

Antarctic organisms have evolved remarkable biological solutions to survive conditions that would be destructive to other organisms. They can withstand air temperatures often permanently well below 0°C (32 degrees Fahrenheit), extreme desiccation in soils with no annual rainfall and extended exposure to high levels of UV-B in the Antarctic summer .

The same adaptations that allow Antarctic organisms to survive may have major practical applications. For instance, our own research , published in 2025, examined the antimicrobial potential of bacteria cultured from eight Antarctic marine invertebrate species, such as sea cucumbers, sea stars and anemones. We found that two strains of these bacteria (Psychrobacter and Pseudomonas) could inhibit the growth of microorganisms of clinical importance such as epidemic methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Micrococcus luteus and Candida albicans in laboratory tests.

As well as Antarctica being a potential source of new drugs and enzymes, its isolated geographical location means that it is a protected ecosystem and is often referred to as " the last great wilderness ." Human activities like tourism and increased scientific activity can risk introducing nonnative microorganisms and diseases to Antarctic communities, which have evolved in relative isolation and may lack resilience against introduced organisms.

Recent research from our laboratory monitored antimicrobial resistance (AMR) caused by humans. Affecting both animals and humans, antimicrobial resistance is a global issue that means some drugs which are used to medicate infections no longer work, leaving some infections untreatable. Our research looked specifically at the extent of AMR around the Rothera Research Station (operated by the U. K. ) on the Antarctic Peninsula.
Overall, our study suggests that treated wastewater has only a limited effect on surrounding marine microbial communities.

However, when we grew these bacteria in our lab, we saw that the bacteria easily adapted to warmer temperatures, which suggests rising temperatures worldwide could change these microbes. This means they may no longer yield some of the potential products we can take advantage of, like cold-adapted enzymes , which work efficiently at room temperature.

articles.title: Gas inside us could fight wound infections, moth study shows
articles.dek: A gas naturally produced by our own bodies could one day help treat skin and wound infections, potentially offering a new approach alongside conventional antibiotics.
paragraphs: A gas naturally produced by our own bodies could one day help treat skin and wound infections, potentially offering a new approach alongside conventional antibiotics.

A new study led by scientists at the University of Reading found that tiny particles releasing nitric oxide helped nine in 10 infected wax moth larvae survive bacterial infections, compared with around six in 10 that were not treated.
Published Nov. 3 in the Journal of Drug Delivery Science and Technology , the findings could give doctors another treatment option for infected wounds that antibiotics struggle to clear.

Vitaliy Khutoryanskiy, a professor at the University of Reading's School of Pharmacy who led the research, said, "With bacteria becoming harder to kill with antibiotics, we urgently need treatments that work in a different way.
"Nitric oxide attacks germs on several fronts at once, so bacteria find it much harder to become resistant. The challenge is to find ways to store it and release it slowly.

"We went beyond killing bacteria in the lab and showed our particles could help infected wax moth larvae survive. Wax moth larvae are becoming increasingly important for testing new treatments, helping us understand how well they work while reducing the need for experiments on mice and rats."

To carry out the study, the research team, which involved scientists from Al-Farabi Kazakh National University (Kazakhstan), first infected wax moth larvae with bacteria that cause skin infections. One hour later, scientists injected each larva with particles that release nitric oxide. Nitric oxide breaks down too quickly to use as a medicine on its own, so the team packed it into particles far smaller than a speck of dust that let it out slowly over several hours.

The larvae were checked for three days, and most deaths among untreated larvae came within the first day. In separate tests in glass flasks, the particles left between 10,000 and 100,000 times fewer bacteria after a day than flasks with no treatment. More studies are needed before the particles could become a treatment for people.

Wax moth larvae were used in this study instead of mice or rats. Each larva weighs about a quarter of a gram (0. 009 ounces), yet its body fights germs in ways similar to those of humans. Scientists can check both whether a treatment is safe and whether it works in a living creature, while relying less on experiments with mammals.

Khutoryanskiy's team is developing tests that use insects, worms and other animals without backbones to study the safety and effectiveness of new medicines and drug delivery systems, helping to reduce reliance on experiments involving mammals.

Nitric oxide–releasing particles increased three-day survival in bacterially infected wax moth larvae to about 90%, compared with 60% without treatment. In laboratory cultures, bacterial counts were 10,000–100,000 times lower after 24 hours than in untreated controls. Further testing is needed before human use.

articles.title: Improved snow model captures Northeast's winter thaws and runoff more accurately
articles.dek: Mountain snow in the Northeast is different. The region's milder, more humid mountain climate shapes winter conditions that are different from those of the western United…
paragraphs: Mountain snow in the Northeast is different. The region's milder, more humid mountain climate shapes winter conditions that are different from those of the western United States. Yet, snow models don't always capture those differences.

In a new study published in the journal Water Resources Research , a team led by the University of Vermont (UVM) has improved a snow model to better represent conditions in the Northeast—using it to explore how snowpack and runoff may respond to changing temperature and precipitation.

The snowpack is an important water resource for northeastern ecosystems and communities. As winters continue to become warmer and wetter, it's important to understand how snow responds to terrain, weather and climate.

"This study is an important step toward an improved understanding of highly vulnerable snowpacks in the face of climatic changes," explains Anna Grunes, the study's lead author and an M. S. graduate in UVM's Civil and Environmental Engineering Department. "With changes to winters that we are seeing all too fast, the Green Mountains of Vermont offer a valuable laboratory to study this. I'm excited to see how continued work with further monitoring infrastructure will support future snow hydrology research in this region."

Many of the Northeast's mountains are situated at intermediate elevations (between 1,000 and 2,000 meters (3,280–6,560 feet)), where snowpacks are dominated by melt-freeze cycles, high-density snow and midwinter thaws. Snow often accumulates and melts more than once per winter, causing flooding and rain-on-snow events .
However, accurately modeling snowpack dynamics is particularly challenging in these warm, wet, lower-elevation environments, as near-freezing temperatures create uncertainty.

Now, a team of researchers from UVM, the U. S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the University of British Columbia has applied a physics-based model to improve representation of midwinter runoff and better inform flood analysis in the region.
While these models have been widely tested and implemented in the western U. S. , few studies have tested the physics-based approach in the Northeast.

The study focused on Mount Mansfield, the highest peak in Vermont's Green Mountain range. The domain extended into the Ranch Brook watershed on the eastern slope of Mount Mansfield, the location of long-term hydrological monitoring and a tributary of the Winooski River that drains into Lake Champlain.

Across this domain, with elevations spanning from 200 to 1,300 meters (660–4,270 feet), the researchers analyzed snowpack and hydrological sensitivity to simulated changes in temperature and precipitation.

They discovered that the snowpack is highly sensitive—most notably at middle elevations (700–900 meters (2,300–2,950 feet)). This elevation band often coincides with the rain-snow line and near-freezing temperatures, where a temperature shift of +1. 1°C can cause a full phase shift from snow to rain, furthering snowmelt.

The team found that the physics-based snow model approach more accurately simulated observations of snow water equivalent (SWE), snow depth, snowpack density and snowmelt-derived runoff. This approach allows researchers to analyze how future changes may affect the at-risk snowpack and hydrological systems in the region.

"Winter snowfall is vital to the Vermont tourism industry, but the snow season is vulnerable to a fast-changing climate," says Dr. Jamie Shanley, research hydrologist (emeritus) for the USGS New England Water Science Center. "This study advances our basic understanding of how the snowpack responds to these changes in the Green Mountains and beyond."

The research team also included Dr. Arne Bomblies, Dr. Donna Rizzo and Dr. Patrick Clemins in UVM's College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences, Dr. Beverley Wemple in UVM's College of Arts & Sciences, Dr. John Hammond with the USGS, and UVM alumnus Dr. Graham Sexstone, now a research scientist with the USGS.

articles.title: Analysis of Inca mummies identifies the drugs used in their most important sacrificial ritual
articles.dek: Archaeologists have performed toxicological analysis on the mummified remains of people sacrificed at mountain shrines across the Inca Empire, revealing the psychoactive…
paragraphs: Archaeologists have performed toxicological analysis on the mummified remains of people sacrificed at mountain shrines across the Inca Empire, revealing the psychoactive substances they consumed before their deaths.

One of the most sacred rituals in the Inca Empire was the capacocha, during which children and young women were sacrificed as an act of veneration for important deities, becoming intermediaries between living people and the divine.
As part of these rituals, the individuals were often given psychoactive substances, possibly as a perceived means to enhance their prophetic abilities.
While the use of psychoactive plants by the Incas is recorded in historical accounts, relatively little is known about the substances consumed during the capacocha.
"Earlier analyses either produced negative results or focused primarily on coca leaves," explains the study's lead author, Dr. Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw.

The preserved bodies of the sacrificed people provide a unique opportunity to investigate this, as chemicals become embedded in the keratin structures of the hair and nails, making them identifiable by toxicological analysis.

"Our aim was to identify a broader range of psychoactive substances administered to the children and to determine whether patterns in their use could provide new insights into how capacocha ceremonies were conducted at different locations," says Socha. "Recent advances in toxicology now allow for the identification of low concentrations of such substances."

The research team performed toxicological analysis on hair and nail samples from eight mummies from several mountains in Peru and Argentina, representing a wide range of sacrificial practices across the Inca Empire. Their results are published in the journal Antiquity .

In all the mummies, they identified cocaine, confirming that the individuals all chewed coca leaves. Coca leaves played an important role in religious beliefs as offerings to the gods, but also could have been a means to help reduce altitude sickness and fatigue during the children's long, arduous journeys up the mountains.

In four mummies, they also found evidence of alcohol consumption, possibly from the corn beer chicha, which is known from historical records to have been given to the children to dull their senses and calm them during the final stage of the ritual.

"One of the most intriguing findings concerns the famous Lady of Ampato, also known as Juanita, in whom we detected traces of harmine," Socha adds. "Harmine is an alkaloid associated with Banisteriopsis species, one of the principal plants traditionally used in the ayahuasca beverage. It may indicate that a harmine-containing beverage had a specific role in ceremonies connected with this particular sacred mountain."

These findings indicate that there were distinct differences between the substances given to each sacrificed individual, suggesting significant variation in how the capacocha was performed across the empire. Ritual practices appear to have been adapted to local religious traditions and to the deities or sacred places involved.

"Five hundred years after these children were sacrificed during one of the most important Inca rituals, new technologies are allowing us to uncover details of their lives and Inca religious practices," Socha concludes. "What we are seeing is that the capacocha was not a single standardized ritual, but rather the Incas appear to have adapted it to different cults and local religious traditions."

articles.title: Telltale furrows: What the Baltic Sea seafloor reveals about bottom trawling
articles.dek: by Kristin Beck, Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW)
paragraphs: by Kristin Beck, Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW)

To what extent does bottom trawling impact the seafloor of the Baltic Sea—and how quickly does it recover? Two new studies from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW) show that the marks on the seafloor provide a much clearer picture of the actual impact than vessel position data alone. Using high-resolution echo sounder measurements and AI, the researchers reveal previously insufficiently recorded impacts and also document surprisingly rapid changes of the seafloor condition. Furthermore, they found strong indications of fishing violations in a marine protected area. The study results were published in the journals Ecological Informatics and Anthropocene .

Bottom trawling is one of the most significant forms of direct human interference with the seafloor. Nets are dragged along the bottom, and heavy net-opening devices—known as "otter boards"—in particular can leave deep furrows. This stirs up sediments, alters habitats and harms benthic organisms. However, it is often difficult to determine the extent to which individual marine areas are affected. Standard methods of monitoring fishing activity based on Automatic Identification System (AIS) vessel data have gaps: Smaller fishing vessels, which play an important role in the western Baltic Sea, are not reliably detected by established monitoring systems.

A team including IOW marine geoscientists Mischa Schönke and Peter Feldens and scientists from the Thünen Institute of Baltic Sea Fisheries has therefore adopted a different approach: Rather than just investigating where fishing vessels have been operating, the researchers analyzed the fishing gear marks on the seafloor. Their research shows how this can be used to record spatial and temporal changes in trawl marks and to gain new insights into the regeneration of the seabed.

"AIS vessel position data tell us where fishing boats have been active. However, they do not necessarily reveal the extent to which the seafloor was actually impacted. The marks in the sediment, on the other hand, provide us with direct evidence of physical changes—even in areas where information on fishing activities is patchy," explains Schönke, lead author of the study published in Ecological Informatics .

Fishing intensity in the western Baltic Sea has changed significantly in recent years. In particular, due to the largely discontinued fishing for cod, bottom trawling declined markedly in many areas from 2022 onward. This presented the researchers with a rare opportunity to investigate how this reduction in fishing pressure is reflected on the seafloor and whether the first signs of ecological recovery are visible.

From 2020 to 2024, the IOW team surveyed an area of up to 4. 7 km² (1. 8 square miles) in the Fehmarn Belt each year using a high-resolution multibeam echo sounder. The device scans the seabed using sound waves and can measure its surface structure down to the centimeter. Based on the volume of detectable trawl furrows, the researchers calculated a so-called Trawling Index, which quantifies the physical damage to the seafloor.

The results revealed significant changes: In 2021, the researchers recorded a furrow volume of approximately 5,067 m³ (179,000 cubic feet) across an area of around 3. 4 km² (1. 3 square miles). By 2022, the volume had fallen to just 1,108 m³ (39,100 cubic feet) across a comparable area—a decline of almost 80%. At the same time, the share of areas with no detectable trawl marks rose from merely 14% in 2021 to as much as 65% in subsequent years.

This trend is not reflected in the AIS vessel position data. This direct comparison of the two methods—the first to be carried out over five consecutive years—thus demonstrates how an assessment based solely on vessel movements can fail to capture the actual changes on the seafloor.

The repeated surveys also show that trawl marks can disappear almost entirely within a year. To investigate whether this also means that the communities on the seafloor recover, the team carried out accompanying sampling of benthic invertebrates such as mussels, worms and crustaceans. The number of individuals, biomass and species composition fluctuated considerably, without revealing any consistent trend over time. While species diversity did show a correlation with trawling intensity, biological recovery has not yet been conclusively demonstrated, as other environmental factors also influence these seafloor communities.

articles.title: Stem cells in deep sleep may point to a secret reserve for lifelong blood renewal
articles.dek: Researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the HI-STEM Stem Cell Institute have discovered a group of particularly long-lived blood stem cells in mice.
paragraphs: Researchers at the German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) and the HI-STEM Stem Cell Institute have discovered a group of particularly long-lived blood stem cells in mice. These cells remain in a dormant state for an exceptionally long time while retaining their ability to generate new blood cells. This newly discovered cell population may be responsible for sustaining blood regeneration and immune defense throughout a mouse's entire life.

Our bodies produce billions of new blood cells every day. These cells transport oxygen, fight pathogens and help stop bleeding. Blood stem cells in the bone marrow are responsible for this vital replenishment. They can renew themselves and produce all types of blood cells—for a lifetime.

To prevent this ability from being exhausted prematurely, many blood stem cells spend a large part of their lives in a sort of dormant state. Only when they are needed do they begin to divide. A team led by researchers at DKFZ and HI-STEM has now identified a special population of stem cells that can remain in this dormant state even longer than previously known blood stem cells.

To identify blood stem cells, researchers use specific protein markers on the cell surface. One of the most important is CD150. Cells lacking CD150 were therefore often not classified as blood stem cells. The new study shows, however, that a particularly interesting population of stem cells is hidden among these very cells, characterized by the surface protein EPCR. The paper is published in the journal Cell Stem Cell .

While other blood stem cells divide at least occasionally, the newly described cells remain inactive for months in mice. After more than 200 days, only about 2% of conventional blood stem cells still exhibited a "quiescence marker." In contrast, about 10% to 15% of the newly characterized stem cells were still positive for this marker. This "deep sleep" could be crucial in enabling the cells to retain their regenerative capacity and ability to produce blood for an exceptionally long time.

Blood stem cells are often awakened from their dormant state by inflammatory signals, allowing the body to produce additional immune cells. However, repeated activation depletes stem cell reserves. In the mice studied, the newly described cell population responded to inflammatory stimuli much more cautiously than conventional blood stem cells.

The Heidelberg team also discovered that the two stem cell groups have different focuses when it comes to forming new blood cells: While the previously known CD150-positive stem cells are more oriented toward the generation of red blood cells and platelets, the newly identified "deep sleepers" show a greater tendency to differentiate into immune cells, particularly lymphocytes.

Nevertheless, both groups can generate all major blood cell types. The researchers confirmed this through transplantation experiments in mice: Even individual cells from the newly characterized population were able to generate all blood cell types and sustain them for life. This ability was maintained even after serial transplantation.
"We show here that blood stem cells do not constitute a uniform cell population but rather comprise different subpopulations with distinct properties and functions," says first author Dawn Lin.

Lead author Andreas Trumpp adds, "Blood stem cells form the basis for stem cell transplants, which are used to treat leukemias and other severe blood disorders. A better understanding of how these cells remain functional even in old age could help further improve these therapies in the future and prevent our blood and immune systems from becoming less effective as we age."

However, the stem cell expert emphasizes that it has not yet been proven that a comparable, particularly long-lived stem cell population exists in humans. "We already have initial evidence of this—that's our next project!"

In mice, EPCR-positive, CD150-negative blood stem cells showed prolonged dormancy, reduced inflammatory responsiveness and a bias toward lymphocyte production. Single cells sustained lifelong production of all major blood cell types and retained this capacity after serial transplantation. A comparable human population remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Hubble Uncovers a Mysterious 93-Billion-Mile Structure Hiding in a Nearby Star System
articles.dek: Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between…
paragraphs: Astronomers have finally detected a mysterious, enormous dust structure in visible light, uncovering new details about what may be the remains of a violent collision between planetary bodies. Known as the “Cat’s Tail,” the feature stretches across as much as 1,000 astronomical units (about 93 billion miles) in the young Beta Pictoris star system.

Located 63 light-years from Earth in the constellation Pictor (which is Latin for “painter”), Beta Pictoris is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rocky debris. The Cat’s Tail was discovered in infrared observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, but had remained hidden from telescopes observing shorter wavelengths. Now, new Hubble Space Telescope images, combined with observations spanning more than 14 years, are helping astronomers investigate its composition, geometry, and possible origins.

“Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while,” said Arin Avsar, a doctoral student at the University of Arizona who led the research.

The explanation may lie in the dust itself. “We think the Cat’s Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it’s made of,” Avsar explained. “It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they’re quite black.”

The observations also suggest that the structure contains microscopic dust grains with an exceptionally porous, fluffy composition. Although the particles are only about a micron across, their internal structure is difficult to explain through conventional models of planetary collisions. “How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that’s part of why we study this feature,” Avsar said.

Beta Pictoris is roughly 20 million years old, making it a valuable laboratory for studying the turbulent environments in which planets develop. Its debris disk contains material left behind from planet formation, including particles produced when larger objects collide.

“The Cat’s Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies – think something like Pluto,” said Avsar, who works with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona’s Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory. Such an impact could have scattered enormous quantities of dust, although the exact process that produced the observed particles remains uncertain.

One possibility is that the impact generated enough heat to transform solid carbon into vapor, which later cooled and formed new particles. “It’s possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that’s how they became so porous,” said Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at Steward Observatory.

The new observations have also changed astronomers’ understanding of the Cat’s Tail’s position in space. Earlier interpretations suggested that the feature extended far behind Beta Pictoris from Earth’s perspective, creating the appearance of a long structure stretching away from the star.

By combining Hubble’s visible-light images with Webb’s infrared observations and computer modeling, the researchers developed a revised picture of its three-dimensional geometry. “We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat’s Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it,” Avsar said. “It’s essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it.”

The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , suggest that much of the structure’s apparent length lies across our field of view rather than extending deep into space. Its precise three-dimensional arrangement remains dependent on the models used to interpret the observations.

Using Hubble in a new observing configuration, the team also identified a previously unseen warp in the dust halo surrounding Beta Pictoris. The distortion may result from the gravitational influence of Beta Pictoris b, one of three known planets in the system and a gas giant approximately 10 times Jupiter’s mass.

articles.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
articles.dek: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight.
paragraphs: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis.

Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space. As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts.

Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit. For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth.

On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade.

NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B.
Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation.

The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963.
Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs.

Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974.

The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities.

To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned.

Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory.

Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities.

To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. articles.title: Scientists Reveal How 60% of Medieval Stories May Have Disappeared Forever
articles.dek: The medieval world may have produced far more stories of knights, legendary heroes, and epic adventures than historians will ever recover.
paragraphs: The medieval world may have produced far more stories of knights, legendary heroes, and epic adventures than historians will ever recover. A new study suggests that up to 60% of medieval chivalric works and more than 95% of their handwritten copies may have disappeared over the centuries.

Jean-Baptiste Camps and colleagues reached these estimates by combining computer simulations with historical evidence from approximately 2,000 medieval manuscripts spanning four centuries. Their research examines how stories survived through repeated copying, why others vanished entirely, and how much of a surviving work’s original history may be missing.

Before the printing press, preserving a literary work depended on scribes making copies by hand. Each new manuscript could introduce accidental errors, deliberate revisions, or adaptations for different audiences. These changes accumulated across generations, producing branching family trees resembling those used to trace evolutionary relationships in biology. Scholars call these textual genealogies stemmata .

The simulations suggest that a work’s earliest years were especially critical. When only a few copies existed, the loss of those manuscripts could cause the entire text to disappear. The authors describe this vulnerable early period as a “danger zone.” Producing numerous copies soon after a work’s creation could substantially improve its chances of surviving for centuries.

The researchers tested several scenarios, including steady copying rates, declining popularity, and sudden destruction of manuscripts during a major crisis. Depending on the scenario, their models estimated that just 1. 4% to 4. 4% of individual manuscripts survived, illustrating how extensive the losses could have been.
The disappearance of manuscripts did more than eliminate entire works. It also erased branches of the textual family trees that connect surviving copies to their origins.

The simulations indicate that surviving manuscripts often descend from later versions rather than directly preserving an author’s original text. The Song of Roland , one of the most famous medieval epics, may be an example. Its earliest form is probably lost, leaving scholars with later versions and rewritings that cannot fully establish what the original contained.

Historical events may have further influenced which stories endured. The Black Death, the Hundred Years’ War, and changing literary tastes could have disrupted manuscript production or contributed to the destruction of existing copies. Although the simulations demonstrate the substantial role chance can play, they do not establish which individual works disappeared because of particular historical events.

“Our results expose the fragility of cultural heritage and offer new tools to understand how randomness, historical contingencies, and human choices have shaped the legacy we inherit today,” the authors write.

articles.title: Earth’s Oceans Were Slowly Suffocating Millions of Years Before a Devastating Mass Extinction
articles.dek: As today’s oceans lose oxygen, Alaskan rocks trace a similar decline that began millions of years before the end-Triassic mass extinction.
paragraphs: As today’s oceans lose oxygen, Alaskan rocks trace a similar decline that began millions of years before the end-Triassic mass extinction.

Dinosaurs survived the end-Triassic mass extinction 201 million years ago, but roughly 60 percent of Earth’s species did not. New evidence from Virginia Tech geologists suggests that the crisis in the oceans began about 8 million years earlier, when oxygen levels in shallow waters started to decline.

Scientists have long linked the extinction to enormous volcanic eruptions that tore apart landmasses, warmed the planet, and triggered widespread environmental changes. As temperatures rise, rocks break down faster, releasing nutrients that contribute to increasing ocean acidity. Warmer seawater also holds less dissolved oxygen, creating conditions that can lead to oxygen-depleted dead zones where marine organisms struggle to survive.
The combination of rising acidity and falling oxygen is “kind of like a one-two punch,” said geochemist Ben Gill. “It wouldn’t have been a very happy place to be.”

Although scientists had previously found evidence of widespread marine oxygen loss around the end-Triassic extinction, much of it came from a limited geographic area. Researchers still lacked a clear understanding of when the decline began and how extensively it affected the oceans. Recent studies had also raised the possibility that environmental conditions started deteriorating far earlier than previously believed.
“It’s a 200-million-year-old cold case,” said Kayla McCabe, a former Virginia Tech geosciences graduate student and first author of the study, published in Communications Earth & Environment .

To investigate, McCabe and her colleagues turned to sedimentary rocks at Grotto Creek in Alaska’s Wrangell–St. Elias National Park. The remote location is accessible only by small aircraft, and the team traveled there in 2017, 2019, and 2022 to collect evidence of ancient ocean conditions.

Sedimentary rocks form as layers of material accumulate over time, preserving chemical traces of the environments in which they were deposited. By comparing layers formed before, during, and after the extinction, the researchers could reconstruct how oxygen conditions changed across millions of years.

The geochemical analyses revealed a prolonged deterioration rather than a sudden collapse. The earlier decline likely placed marine ecosystems under stress long before the main extinction event. Conditions then worsened considerably during the extinction itself, with the rock record showing a much more severe loss of oxygen. The findings indicate that oxygen starvation became a major contributor to the disappearance of marine species.

What triggered the initial decline remains uncertain. The massive volcanic eruptions associated with the end-Triassic extinction have long been considered a major cause of the environmental catastrophe, but the newly identified timeline raises questions about what was happening millions of years beforehand.
“There’s evidence of another volcanic province that roughly lines up with this time interval,” Gill said. “But we’re in the very beginning of trying to understand what happened.”

The ancient rock record also offers a way to examine the potential consequences of environmental changes unfolding today. Modern oceans are experiencing rising temperatures, acidification, and declining oxygen levels. Ocean deoxygenation is an ongoing concern, including in coastal environments such as the Chesapeake Bay .

Although the ancient and modern circumstances are different, understanding how warming and oxygen depletion affected marine life in the past could help scientists anticipate the combined pressures facing ocean ecosystems today.

“Earth has run this experiment in the past. We have evidence that the climate gets warmer, and then all these other knock-on effects come afterwards,” Gill said. “It gives us some sense of what we can expect to happen.”

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Powerful New Way To Destroy Toxic “Forever Chemicals”
articles.dek: Scientists have developed a new way to destroy toxic “forever chemicals” in water rather than simply filter them out.
paragraphs: Scientists have developed a new way to destroy toxic “forever chemicals” in water rather than simply filter them out. During a 58-day experiment, the system removed more than 90% of each of six PFAS compounds and stripped away approximately 83% of their fluorine, providing evidence that the pollutants were being chemically broken down.

PFAS are widely used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, food packaging, and firefighting foam. Their exceptional durability also allows them to persist in soil, water, wildlife, and the human body. Exposure to certain PFAS has been linked to cancer, thyroid disorders, immune system problems, and reproductive health risks.

Conventional treatments capture PFAS using filters, membranes, or other materials, leaving contaminated waste that must still be managed. Researchers at Arizona State University and their collaborators instead developed a system that attacks the chemicals’ molecular structure.
“PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” said Bruce Rittmann, director of the Biodesign Swette Center for Environmental Biotechnology.

The challenge lies in the carbon-fluorine bonds that make PFAS exceptionally stable. “It’s called the strongest bond in organic chemistry,” Rittmann said. With fluorine atoms shielding the carbon backbone, ordinary degradation processes struggle to attack the molecules. “There’s really no place to get a start to break it down,” he explained.

The researchers created tiny membrane fibers coated with palladium nanoparticles. Hydrogen gas travels through the fibers to the palladium, which activates the hydrogen and helps it break carbon-fluorine bonds in PFAS molecules approaching from the surrounding water.
“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said.

The system builds on earlier membrane technology that supplies hydrogen to pollutant-degrading bacteria. In the new approach, palladium replaces the microbes. During continuous testing, the technology successfully treated all six PFAS compounds examined. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six,” Rittmann said. “It’s a universal mechanism.”
The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .

PFAS contamination affects groundwater, wastewater, soil, and food supplies. Particularly high concentrations occur near landfills, airports, military bases, and facilities where PFAS-containing firefighting foams have been used.
“We all have PFAS in us,” Rittmann said. “They stay in the environment. They move up the food chain, and so they’re a big legacy problem.”

Although the 58-day test demonstrated sustained treatment, scaling up the technology presents challenges, particularly the cost of palladium. “Palladium is expensive,” Rittmann said. “It’s around $50,000 a kilogram” (about $22,700 per pound).

The researchers are working to reduce palladium requirements and explore combining the technology with existing filtration systems. They are also developing hybrid membranes that pair palladium with pollutant-degrading bacteria, allowing contaminants to be attacked through different mechanisms. “We’ve shown that this works too,” Rittmann said.

articles.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
articles.dek: Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
paragraphs: Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon!
November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky!
The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th.
Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate.
Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile.

Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer.
To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can.
Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together.
They’ll appear about 1. 2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby.
Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side.
Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways.
This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it!

articles.title: NASA Invites Media to Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Station Resupply Launch
articles.dek: Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
paragraphs: Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA.

The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a. m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA.

Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U. S. media. The application deadline for U. S. citizens is 11:59 p. m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at:

Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail. nasa. gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468.

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions.

Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U. S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space.

For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy , NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars.

articles.title: A Simple Tongue Exercise Could Hold the Key to Fighting the Devastating Effects of ALS
articles.dek: Researchers at the University of Missouri have uncovered a promising way to help surviving nerve cells compensate for damage caused by ALS and other motor neuron diseases.
paragraphs: Researchers at the University of Missouri have uncovered a promising way to help surviving nerve cells compensate for damage caused by ALS and other motor neuron diseases.

The loss of tongue control in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) can affect far more than speech. It can make swallowing increasingly difficult and interfere with breathing during sleep. Now, researchers at the University of Missouri have discovered that tongue exercise can increase the activity of surviving nerve cells in a preclinical model, potentially offering a new approach to preserving these essential functions.

ALS, also called Lou Gehrig’s disease, progressively damages the motor neurons responsible for muscle movement and currently has no cure. However, not all neurons controlling the tongue are lost, particularly during the early stages. Researchers are investigating whether these surviving cells can compensate for damaged neurons and help maintain muscle function.

The findings center on neuroplasticity, the nervous system’s ability to adapt to damage or changing conditions. In the preclinical model, tongue exercise increased the activity of surviving motor neurons, suggesting that targeted training may help the remaining cells compensate for those lost to disease. Scientists have not yet determined exactly how exercise produces this response.

“This adaptation is called neuroplasticity, meaning the nervous system changes how it operates to compensate for damage, and this finding offers hope for those with motor neuron diseases,” said Nicole Nichols, an associate professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and coauthor of the study. “By boosting the activity of the surviving neurons, we can help preserve the quality of life for those with ALS, spinal muscular atrophy and other motor neuron diseases.”

The tongue plays a central role in speaking, moving food during swallowing, and keeping the airway open during sleep. As the muscles weaken in people with ALS, eating can become difficult enough to require a feeding tube. Reduced tongue muscle function can also contribute to sleep apnea, a condition in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep.

“For those with ALS, preserving swallowing function not only reduces the chance of developing sleep apnea, it could also mean the difference between needing a feeding tube or continuing to eat normally,” she said. “That’s incredibly meaningful for quality of life.”

Although the results are promising, the benefits have so far been demonstrated only in a preclinical model. Researchers now want to understand the biological mechanisms that allow tongue exercise to increase neuronal activity. Identifying those mechanisms could eventually support the development of medications that reproduce the effects of exercise without requiring patients to perform physical training.

“If we can figure out exactly how and why the tongue exercise helps the remaining neurons function better, that can help the development of treatments that mimic the benefits,” Nichols said. “For example, for someone with a very poor prognosis who may not be able to do tongue exercise, is there an injectable that we can give them that would activate those surviving motor neurons to improve their function? While both tongue exercise as a therapy and an injectable would require human clinical trials in the future, this finding is a step in the right direction.”
Nichols and her colleagues hope to advance tongue exercise toward human clinical trials within the next several years through collaborations at Mizzou’s NextGen Precision Health.

articles.title: Why Are Men Twice As Likely To Develop Parkinson’s? Scientists Discover a Hidden Clue in the Brain
articles.dek: Scientists have identified sex-specific differences in gene activity within brain cells that may help explain why Parkinson’s disease affects men more frequently than women.
paragraphs: Scientists have identified sex-specific differences in gene activity within brain cells that may help explain why Parkinson’s disease affects men more frequently than women.

Men are 1. 5 to 2 times more likely than women to develop Parkinson’s disease, yet the biological reasons remain poorly understood. New research suggests that differences in gene activity within the brain’s support cells may help explain why the condition affects the sexes differently.

The findings, presented at the Federation of European Neuroscience Societies (FENS) Forum 2026, are based on brain tissue from 73 people with Parkinson’s disease (28 women and 45 men) and 24 people without the condition (9 women and 15 men). Researchers examined five brain regions, identifying cellular changes shared by both sexes as well as distinct patterns in men and women.

The strongest differences appeared in two types of glial cells, which support and protect neurons. In astrocytes, gene activity related to mitochondria, the structures that produce cellular energy, differed between sexes. In oligodendrocytes, researchers identified differences involving genes responsible for producing and maintaining myelin, the protective coating surrounding nerve fibers. These patterns appeared across the brain regions studied.

Professor Julia Schulze-Hentrich of Saarland University in Germany, who led the research, explained: “We looked at differences in gene expression individually in all cells of the brain – neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia – in healthy brains and in PD brains in men and women. We studied five brain regions and found that PD causes common changes in the brain, regardless of sex. All these cells in the five regions, showed signs of being under stress. They switched on proteins that help damaged proteins fold correctly, called ‘chaperones’. However, we also found important differences between men and women in gene activity in some cells and some brain regions.”

“This shows that PD triggers some shared ‘stress responses’ in everyone’s brain cells, but also there are differences between men and women at the cellular level, especially in how the brain ‘support’ cells manage energy and protect nerve connections. Our findings help to explain why symptoms and disease progression in Parkinson’s differ between men and women. Eventually, they may lead to more personalized treatments rather than treating all patients with PD as biologically identical,” said Prof. Schulze-Hentrich.

Parkinson’s disease causes progressive brain damage and affects approximately 9. 4 million people worldwide. About 90% of cases are thought to involve a combination of genetic variation and environmental or lifestyle influences. Men not only develop the disease more frequently but also tend to experience faster cognitive decline and worsening difficulties with everyday activities.

“The higher prevalence of Parkinson’s disease in men suggests that sex-dependent biology may influence vulnerability. Therefore, studying sex differences may help identifying disease mechanisms that would be hidden in analyses that pool men and women together,” said Prof. Schulze-Hentrich, who is affiliated with Saarland University’s Center for Gender-Specific Biology and Medicine (CGMB).

The investigation builds on an earlier study involving 71 agricultural workers with early Parkinson’s and 147 healthy participants. Researchers found changes in DNA methylation across 69 genomic regions in women with Parkinson’s, compared with just two in men. DNA methylation regulates gene activity without altering the underlying DNA sequence, functioning much like a dimmer switch.

“These findings suggested that a person’s genetic makeup influences these DNA methylation changes, and that interaction with environmental exposures, such as to pesticides, may also contribute to the development of Parkinson’s disease,” Prof. Schulze-Hentrich said.

The new study extended this work by examining gene expression in individual types of brain cells. Although it identified differences associated with biological sex, it did not establish that those differences directly cause the higher rate of Parkinson’s in men.

The study’s relatively small sample size limits its conclusions, and larger investigations are needed. The findings also reinforce the need to examine men and women separately in Parkinson’s research, which has historically focused heavily on neurons and male subjects.

“Most importantly, our results indicate that it is crucial to recognize that biology varies between the sexes in PD research and that, wherever possible, researchers should analyze data separately in males and females instead of pooling everyone together. This is crucial to see whether an association, effect or outcome differs by sex. It also helps identify gaps in evidence because many studies still underreport or pool sex-specific outcomes.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a New Type of Depression That Common Antidepressants May Miss
articles.dek: For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.
paragraphs: For some people with hard-to-treat depression, the body’s internal clock may help explain why standard antidepressants fall short.

University of Sydney researchers have identified a proposed subtype called “circadian depression,” marked by disrupted sleep and daily rhythms. It accounted for nearly a quarter of participants in a study of more than 10,000 Australians with severe, recurrent or persistent depression.

The findings, published in the British Journal of Psychiatry , suggest that recognizing this pattern could help clinicians identify people who may benefit from treatments targeting the body clock earlier in their care.

“Our research has identified circadian depression as a new subtype, affecting around a quarter of people in our study into those with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression,” said first author Dr. Emiliana Tonini, from the university’s Brain and Mind Centre .

Using clinical and genetic information from the nationwide Australian Genetics of Depression Study , the researchers classified nearly 25 percent (2,604 participants) as having circadian depression. Its features included seasonal episodes, sleeping longer when depressed, waking up exhausted, and a tendency to stay up late.

These symptoms point toward the circadian system, the body’s internal 24-hour timekeeping network that regulates sleep and wakefulness. The researchers identified genetic characteristics of the subtype that could help explain why treatments aimed at other brain pathways are less effective.

Participants with circadian depression were more likely to have developed depression earlier in life and experienced more severe symptoms (such as mania and higher levels of suicidal thoughts). They also had greater genetic susceptibility to inflammatory and cardiovascular conditions and major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD.

“Depression is not a uniform illness, and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes means that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them,” Tonini said.

SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are commonly offered as initial treatments for depression. People with the circadian subtype reported less benefit and more side effects from these medications.

The researchers suggest that this group may respond better to behavioral and medical therapies targeting the brain circuits involved in circadian rhythms. Options include light therapy, melatonin, and antidepressants that act on melatonin pathways.

Co-senior author Dr. Jacob Crouse, from the Brain and Mind Centre, said, “Because circadian depression is linked to people’s internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation.
“For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances.”

For young people, identifying this pattern early could help avoid unsuccessful initial treatments and additional side effects, according to Professor Ian Hickie, Co-Director of the Brain and Mind Centre and a clinical psychiatrist.
“We really want young people to receive the most appropriate treatment early in their course of illness.

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Uncovers Case of Missing Oxygen in Nearby Dwarf Galaxies
articles.dek: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood.
paragraphs: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood. In a paper published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing.
Simulations predict that significantly more oxygen, a tracer of a wider set of heavy elements, should reside in these galaxies. So where did it go?

“Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies. We know that the oxygen had to be inside of the galaxies at some point in the past, so the oxygen must have been ejected,” said co-investigator Grace Telford, assistant professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Utah. “And to do that, you need energy from massive stars and supernova explosions to drive material out of the host galaxies and into the space between galaxies.”

Galactic winds unleashed by supernovae are apparently more effective at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current models predict, according to the new study. The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars.

In the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, scientists traced the oxygen to understand how it is distributed inside stars, in the gas between stars, and in the space between galaxies. But, of all the elements in the galaxies, why study oxygen?

Oxygen, the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium, is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood — making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy.

“So, it’s really for practical reasons that we’ve chosen oxygen,” said Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, GLOW principal investigator and mission head of the Science Operations Center for NASA’s newly launched, panoramic Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, Maryland. She also is an associate professor at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey.

“Oxygen is one of the primary elements formed by stars. Being able to trace how much oxygen gets made, and then how much is distributed inside and outside of galaxies, helps us understand galaxy evolution,” said McQuinn. “It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium.”

The study used archival optical imaging data from Hubble to resolve stellar populations and determine star-formation histories and compositions. Along with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground-based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, the researchers analyzed 37 nearby dwarf galaxies to trace oxygen atoms produced by stars.

The team wanted to understand how oxygen is distributed across the stars, gas, and dust in the galaxies. These dwarf galaxies were selected because their masses fall in the range where simulations and theory predict that an increasing amount of their oxygen will be expelled from the galaxies via supernovae explosions. These 37 galaxies also are all close enough for Hubble to resolve their individual stars. That’s not true for the vast majority of known dwarf galaxies, which are too far away for this kind of study.

Although astronomers already suspected that galaxies expel a large fraction of oxygen and other heavy elements, an open question has been where these metals end up. A previous study from 2014 addressed this question for Milky Way-like, star-forming galaxies, finding that these galaxies lost a large fraction of their oxygen, some of which is found in the diffuse haloes of gas surrounding galaxies outside their disks, called the circumgalactic medium.

In the GLOW study, McQuinn and her team extended this research to low-mass galaxies across a wide range of masses and environments. While previous teams have measured oxygen in the circumgalactic medium of dwarf galaxies, it is still unclear if most of the missing oxygen is in this region, or if it has been completely ejected from the galaxy’s surroundings.

articles.title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor
articles.dek: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem.
paragraphs: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more , and 14. 6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated , and some are two decades old . Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed , including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding , even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives , how well the building holds up , whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner . They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes , and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.
Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy , and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s , and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes , improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.
Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.
Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.
